newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Workers across Russia struggle without pay.
newsitem.headline: Workers across Russia struggle without pay.

text.p: Millions of Russians, still struggling to survive in the tough new world of a market economy, have not been paid for months and the volume of wage arrears is rising all the time, a newspaper said on Wednesday.
Trud newspaper -- the name means labour -- said wage arrears had risen by four trillion roubles ($740 million) to 40.23 trillion in the two weeks from September 9.
"The situation has become really tense," the newspaper said.

"A vast army of people -- 16-18 million Russians or almost a quarter of the working population -- have not received what they are owed for their labour... Poverty is mercilessly taking tens of millions of Russians by the throat."
The wage arrears, among public and private sector workers, are part of a circle of non-payments affecting virtually every corner of the Russian economy.
The government and newly privatised firms ignore their bills, workers go for months without pay and power companies struggle to supply factories because they have not been paid.
The wage arrears have prompted strikes across Russia, especially in the Arctic and in the Far East.

"Our citizens, quite justifiably, protest against the practice which has grown in recent years of them not receiving the wages they have earned," parliament chairman Gennady Seleznyov told deputies at the first session of the State Duma lower house of parliament since the summer recess.
"There is a serious financial crisis, not just in separate branches of industry...but in key state institutions such as the army, law enforcement, education, science and health."
Figures released last month showed that almost 30 million people, or 20 percent of the Russian population, were living below the subsistence level.
Official figures showed that wages averaged 850,000 roubles ($160) a month in August, but the data hide a vast black economy, untaxed and virtually unreported.
Wages have risen in dollar terms since Russia launched its economic reforms in January 1992, but the figures provide cold comfort for those who have not been paid at all.
Trud, in its front-page article, highlighted the misery of people who had not received their wages.
"Winter is coming and we do not have boots or coats, and we do not have anything to eat," the paper said, quoting a letter from Maria Kolesnikova, a reader from the Volgograd region.
"It is not easy for me to write this -- it is like begging, it is such a disgrace -- and I am doing this for the first time in my life, but we are in great trouble, on the very edge."

The newspaper added: "Those seeking where to borrow money for a piece of bread can only smile bitterly at talk of a 'decrease in the number of poor people'. In regional elections they will vote for anyone who is not backed by Moscow."
Noting that a communist took power in local elections in the Amur region near the border with China, the newspaper said:

"It is not because the Bolshevik spirit is so strong in the region, it is that people can no longer stand poverty, privation and hardship. They did not vote for the communists but against the unbelievably cruel social policy of the authorities."
The communists, the largest party in the Duma, are hoping that a string of elections for regional governors will strengthen their position in the Federation Council upper house.
($ 1 = 5,420 roubles)
